subChunks.title: Obituaries, Notices & the Genealogical Newspaper
subChunks.hookHtml: Newspapers recorded the texture of daily life that no official record ever captured — births announced with the mother's maiden name, deaths commemorated with full family lists, criminal proceedings naming victims and witnesses, and social columns tracking who visited whom and when. For many families, a well-researched newspaper obituary gives more genealogical detail than any official record. Learning to search digitised newspaper archives is one of the skills that most reliably breaks research brick walls.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What newspapers contain for genealogists

Historical newspapers are rich in the following genealogically useful content:

  • Birth announcements: often give the mother's maiden name, the father's occupation, and sometimes the attending physician. In many communities, birth announcements in newspapers are the only pre-registration record of a birth.
  • Marriage notices: frequently include both families' names, the officiating minister, the wedding location, and sometimes a list of witnesses or guests — all potential relatives.
  • Obituaries: the genealogical goldmine. A Victorian or Edwardian obituary can be more complete than a family group sheet — listing spouse, children by name (daughters with married surnames), surviving siblings, parents, place of birth, and length of residence in the area. The funeral notice often names the pallbearers, who were typically relatives or close friends.
  • Court reports: quarter sessions, assizes, and local magistrates' courts reported in detail, naming defendants, plaintiffs, witnesses, and solicitors. A civil dispute over a will or land boundary may name family members and relationships that appear nowhere in official records.
  • Local news and social columns: 'Mrs Patrick Walsh of Cork Street has returned from a visit to her sister in Liverpool' tells you she has a sister in Liverpool. Social columns track family connections across communities.
  • Shipping news and passenger lists: 19th-century newspapers frequently published the names of arriving and departing passengers, sometimes more completely than official manifests.

Searching effectively — the challenge of OCR

Most digitised newspapers are made searchable via Optical Character Recognition (OCR) — software that reads the printed text from scanned images and converts it to searchable text. OCR quality varies greatly by the age and condition of the paper. A Victorian newspaper with faded ink and deteriorated paper may have OCR accuracy of only 70–80%, meaning roughly 20–30% of words are misread. The implications:

  • Search by phonetic variants of your surname — a name missed in one search may be found in another
  • Search by first name alone if the surname fails — "Patrick" plus a date range and county may recover a result that "Walsh" missed
  • Browse specific newspaper issues directly when the date window is narrow (e.g. you know a death occurred in a specific month)
  • Some platforms allow you to correct OCR errors — correcting the text improves future searches for everyone

Obituary analysis — extracting maximum information

When you find an obituary, read it systematically for these elements:

  1. Age and birthplace — often given: "aged 72, a native of County Cork"
  2. Occupation and length of residence — where they lived and for how long, narrowing the search window
  3. Surviving family members — spouse (with maiden name if recently married), children (daughters with married surnames), and sometimes siblings
  4. Predeceasing relatives — "is survived by his wife and three children; he was predeceased by his wife Bridget (née Murphy) in 1902" — suddenly the first wife's maiden name appears
  5. Funeral arrangements — the officiating minister names the church; the burial location gives the cemetery; the pallbearers are named
  6. Obituary source — which newspaper, which date, which page, which edition. Cite this precisely.

Trade directories and almanacs

Before the telephone directory, trade directories were the standard reference for who was doing business where. For genealogists:

  • Kelly's Directories (England): annual county directories listing tradespeople, farmers, and professional men by parish; invaluable for tracking a family year by year between censuses
  • Pigot's, Slater's, and White's Directories: earlier English directories; coverage from c.1820
  • Thom's Irish Almanac and Official Directory: annual Irish directory from 1844
  • US city directories: annual directories for most US cities from roughly 1840; often earlier than census and vital registration; available on Ancestry (US City Directories collection)

City directories are particularly useful in the US for the periods between censuses: a man who appears in the 1880 census and the 1900 census may appear in annual directories from 1881 to 1899, tracking his address, occupation, and sometimes the names of family members living with him. Annual directories can also detect when a widow first appears listed alone — indicating the death of a husband.

storyBeats.text: Theodora turns a laptop screen toward you — it shows a page from an 1887 Manchester Evening News, densely printed in columns. She zooms in on a short column in the bottom right: 'Deaths.'

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Twenty lines. That is all a Victorian death notice often gives you — twenty lines, buried at the bottom of the Deaths column. But those twenty lines may give you what ten years of census searching did not. 'Patrick Walsh, beloved husband of Mary (née Riordan), father of Thomas, Bridget, and James; also beloved son of the late Michael Walsh and Catherine (née Sullivan) of Kilmihil, County Clare, Ireland.' Maiden names. Parents. Home county in Ireland. All in twenty lines.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The challenge is finding it. OCR — optical character recognition — reads the printed text from the scanned page and makes it searchable. But Victorian newspaper print was not designed for computers. Faded ink, deteriorated paper, close-set type — the OCR accuracy may be 70 to 80 percent. A Walsh misread as Malsh, a Murphy misread as Muiphy. Your search fails and you conclude the notice does not exist. But it does. Browse the specific issue. Search by first name alone. Search phonetic variants. The notice is there; the algorithm just could not read it.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And do not overlook the city directories. Between census years — between 1880 and 1890, between 1900 and 1910 — a family may appear in annual city directories every year, their address shifting slightly, the occupation changing, a wife's name appearing alone after the husband's death. The US City Directories collection on Ancestry covers most major American cities from around 1840. It is one of the most underused genealogical resources in existence.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor newspaper research skills

Retrieve from memory:

  • Name three types of genealogically useful content found in historical newspapers beyond death notices.
  • What is OCR and why does it cause problems in newspaper searches?
  • What are Kelly's Directories and how can they bridge gaps between censuses?
  • Name one free US and one free Australian newspaper archive.
  • What five elements should you extract from a Victorian obituary?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Three genealogically useful newspaper contents beyond death notices: (1) birth announcements (often give mother's maiden name and father's occupation); (2) court reports (name parties in civil and criminal cases, potentially identifying family relationships); (3) social columns (track family connections and movements across communities).

OCR (Optical Character Recognition) is software that reads printed text from scanned images and converts it to searchable text. Victorian and Edwardian newspapers often have poor OCR accuracy (70–80%) because faded ink, deteriorated paper, and close-set type confuse the software — causing names to be misread and thus missed in keyword searches.

Kelly's Directories are annual county directories for England listing tradespeople, farmers, and professional men by parish. They can be searched year by year between census dates (e.g. 1881–1889 between the 1881 and 1891 censuses) to track a family's address and occupation, and to detect when a widow first appears listed alone.

Free US newspaper archive: Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov). Free Australian: Trove (trove.nla.gov.au).

Five elements to extract from a Victorian obituary: (1) age and birthplace of the deceased; (2) occupation and length of residence; (3) surviving family members (spouse with maiden name, children with married surnames); (4) predeceasing relatives; (5) funeral arrangements (minister, cemetery, pallbearers).
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Analysing an obituary for genealogical data

Extract every genealogical fact from the following obituary excerpt and classify each fact as: (a) directly useful for your tree; (b) a lead requiring further research; or (c) context only. Then write a list of follow-up searches the obituary suggests.

"WALSH — On Monday, 14 March 1887, at 27 Cork Street, Manchester, Patrick Walsh, aged 62, beloved husband of Mary (née Riordan), dearly loved father of Thomas (Manchester), James (Liverpool), Bridget Murphy of Cork, and Ellen Crawford of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA, and dear son of the late Michael Walsh and Catherine (née Sullivan) of Kilmihil, County Clare, Ireland. Funeral arrangements: Thursday 17 March, St Patrick's Church, Manchester. Officiating: Rev. Father O'Brien. Interment at Weaste Cemetery. Pallbearers: John Riordan, Michael Murphy, James Crawford, Thomas Kelly. The family requests no flowers."
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Genealogical data extracted:

(a) Directly useful:
- Patrick Walsh: died 14 March 1887, aged 62, at 27 Cork Street, Manchester. Born approximately 1825.
- Mary Walsh: wife; née Riordan.
- Patrick's parents: Michael Walsh and Catherine Sullivan; from Kilmihil, County Clare, Ireland. Both deceased by 1887.
- Children: Thomas Walsh (Manchester); James Walsh (Liverpool); Bridget Murphy — married surname Murphy, location Cork; Ellen Crawford — married surname Crawford, location Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
- Burial: Weaste Cemetery, Manchester; funeral 17 March 1887, St Patrick's Church.

(b) Leads requiring further research:
- John Riordan (pallbearer): likely a relative of Mary (née Riordan) — possibly her brother or cousin. Search Manchester directories and census for John Riordan.
- Michael Murphy (pallbearer): likely related to daughter Bridget Murphy — possibly her husband or father-in-law. Search Cork records for Murphy/Walsh connections.
- James Crawford (pallbearer): likely related to daughter Ellen Crawford — possibly her husband. Search Philadelphia records for James Crawford married to Ellen Walsh.
- Thomas Kelly (pallbearer): unknown connection. May be a neighbour, workmate, or more distant relative.
- Kilmihil, County Clare: Patrick's parents' home parish. Search Kilmihil Catholic parish registers (irishgenealogy.ie) for Walsh family and births of Patrick c.1825.
- Weaste Cemetery: apply for the burial register entry to confirm date of death and grave number.

(c) Context only:
- Rev. Father O'Brien: confirms Catholic faith. St Patrick's Manchester is a known Irish Catholic parish.
- Address 27 Cork Street: check Manchester street directories for occupation, length of residence.

questions.questionHtml: Which free online archive holds historical US newspapers from 1770 to 1963?
questions.explanationHtml: Chronicling America is the Library of Congress's free digitised newspaper archive, covering US papers from 1770 to 1963 and fully text-searchable. The British Newspaper Archive covers UK papers (subscription). Trove covers Australian materials (free). Newspapers.com is a subscription service (Ancestry company) covering US and some international papers.

questions.questionHtml: You are searching for the obituary of a Margaret Kelly who died in Chicago in approximately 1895. Your search for 'Kelly' finds no results in the Chronicling America newspaper archive. What is the best next step?
options: Browse the specific Chicago newspapers issue by issue for the months surrounding the expected death date, and try variant spellings such as 'Kelley', 'Kellie', and 'Kell' — OCR errors may have caused the surname to be misread
Conclude the obituary was never published — not all deaths received newspaper coverage
Switch to searching the GRO death index instead of newspapers
The 1890 US census destruction means no records survive for Chicago families from the 1890s
questions.correctAnswer: Browse the specific Chicago newspapers issue by issue for the months surrounding the expected death date, and try variant spellings such as 'Kelley', 'Kellie', and 'Kell' — OCR errors may have caused the surname to be misread
questions.explanationHtml: OCR misreads are the most common cause of failed newspaper searches. Victorian newspaper print quality and the limitations of OCR software mean that a name present in the paper may not be searchable as typed. The strategies: search phonetic variants of the surname; search by first name only with a date range; browse the death notices column of the relevant newspaper issues directly. Chicago had multiple major newspapers in the 1890s (Chicago Tribune, Chicago Inter Ocean, etc.) and local neighbourhood papers — try multiple titles.

questions.questionHtml: A US city directory from 1887 lists 'Mary Walsh, widow' at an address where 'Patrick Walsh, labourer' appeared in the 1885 and 1886 directories. What can a careful researcher conclude from this pattern?
options: Patrick Walsh likely died between the publication of the 1886 and 1887 directories — this narrows the death year and suggests searching death records and newspaper obituaries for that window
Mary Walsh divorced Patrick Walsh sometime in that period
Directory listings are too unreliable to draw any inference about death or separation
The two listings are unrelated — different Patrick and Mary Walshs at the same address
questions.correctAnswer: Patrick Walsh likely died between the publication of the 1886 and 1887 directories — this narrows the death year and suggests searching death records and newspaper obituaries for that window
questions.explanationHtml: City directories were compiled annually, typically in the autumn or spring. A man appearing as head of household in one year and a widow appearing at the same address the next year strongly suggests death in the intervening period. This is a reliable death-date narrowing technique, especially for the period before complete vital registration. The researcher should now search death certificates or GRO death index for Patrick Walsh in that state and county for the 12–18 month window between directory compilations, and search newspapers for an obituary in the same window.
